NOT PROVABLE
Open in general, but there exist models of set theory where the result is false.
Let $\mathfrak{m}$ be an infinite cardinal and $G$ be a graph with chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$. Is it true that, for every infinite cardinal $\mathfrak{n}< \mathfrak{m}$, there exists a subgraph of $G$ with chromatic number $\mathfrak{n}$?
#739: [Er81]
graph theory | 
chromatic number
A question of Galvin [Ga73], who proved that this is true with $\mathfrak{m}=\aleph_0$. Galvin also proved that the stronger version of this statement, in which the subgraph is induced, implies $2^{\mathfrak{k}}<2^{\mathfrak{n}}$ for all cardinals $\mathfrak{k}<\mathfrak{n}$. 
Komjáth [Ko88b] proved it is consistent that\[2^{\aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_1}=2^{\aleph_2}=\aleph_3\]and that there exist graphs which fail this property (with $\mathfrak{m}=\aleph_2$ and $\mathfrak{n}=\aleph_1$).
Shelah [Sh90] proved that, assuming the axiom of constructibility, the answer is yes with $\mathfrak{m}=\aleph_2$ and $\mathfrak{n}=\aleph_1$.
It remains open whether the answer to this question is yes assuming the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis, for example.

 Komjáth, P. Consistency results on infinite graphs. Israel J. Math. 61, 285–294 (1988). https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02772573
The first sentence of the abstract is the following:
"Consistently there exist $\aleph_2$-chromatic graphs with no $\aleph_1$-chromatic subgraphs."
The subgraphs here are not just the induced ones (as that previous result in mentioned in the introduction). The consistency is with $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_3$. I guess the problem is likely still open in the purest sense.

 We *could* add new categories to the problem status: "Not disprovable", "Not provable", and "Undecidable"; seems like this result would then place the problem in the "not provable" category (assuming set theory is consistent, of course). Though this seems like overkill for a single problem... if it turns out that there is a second problem whose answers or partial results depend on additional set theoretic axioms then I might introduce these categories.

 There is at least one other candidate in the new [1067], whose answer is independent of ZFC. Other examples are [474] and [736]. (It has been speculated that the answer to [508] might also be independent of ZFC.)
The trouble is that there is no single tag appropriate for all of these - 'Independent' works for some, 'Not disprovable' for others.
I'm sure there will be many more candidates as well - Erdős' problems on set theory and infinite graphs are probably the largest unexplored source of problems that I haven't really gone into yet.
